goal: Read a river seen two ways and open the question of how experience changes a narrator.
note: Twain, Two Views of the Mississippi (g12-u1-01), first half. Hook first, then unmarked retrieval of e11-narrative, e11-process and e11-reading-band. Privacy: invented experience is an equal writing option; no disclosure required.

goal: Trace significance, viewpoint, pacing and reflection in a model memoir.
note: Finish Twain. Retrieve e11-argument and e11-routine-writing; start the daily text-dependent exit ticket and reading log. Teach W.3a/b: situation/significance, narrator/viewpoint, smooth progression, dialogue, pacing, description, reflection and multiple plot lines.

goal: Read how Addams orders uncertainty toward a reflective close.
note: Read Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House chapter 4 (g12-u1-02), whole assigned chapter. Teach W.3c/e: connected sequence, tone/outcome and reflective conclusion. Retrieve e11-academic-words; begin source-and-sentence word log and independent book selection. Week 1, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: reflect / reflection / reflective (Latin flect/flex; re-; -ion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. First retrieve e11-word-strategies (grade 11 families/word-change work) for two minutes from the supplied prior-grade log; the pending shared band list is not assumed taught. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Use a model narrative to connect telling detail with purpose and audience.
note: Read Curio Class Model reflective essay (g12-u1-04, to write). Teach W.3d and W.4: precise sensory detail, coherent development/organization/style for task, purpose and audience. Retrieve e11-usage-conventions. Student may choose imagined material.

goal: Write a two-text paragraph that tests a familiar reading of a poem against its words.
note: Read Frost, The Road Not Taken (g12-u1-03), whole, beside Addams chapter 4. W.9a/b: literary word/tone analysis and nonfiction idea analysis in one paragraph. Retrieve e11-seminar; teach preparation, civil democratic norms, own goal/deadline/roles, probing, all positions, synthesis, contradictions and further research, SL.1a to d.

goal: Resolve contested usage and edit hyphenation, capitalization, punctuation and spelling.
note: Read draft sentences beside the 1926 usage guide and current dictionary notes. Teach L.1a/b and L.2a/b: changing/contested convention, reference consultation, defended choice for audience, hyphenation and spelling. Retrieve the grade 11 sentence routine on Twain syntax. Week 2, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: reflect / reflection / reflective (Latin flect/flex; re-; -ion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Discuss what Twain and Addams gain and lose through experience.
note: Reread Twain and Addams. Partner exchange then teacher-led seminar; prepare evidence, test positions and name research needed. Practice only; scored discussion evidence is gathered on day 14.

goal: Draft an opening and scene that develop a problem and its significance.
note: Read the model opening then student drafts. Practise W.3a/b/d: viewpoint, dialogue, pacing, sensory detail and connected plot lines. Privacy choices continue. Practice can fold into days 7 and 9. Conference rota: ten of 30 learners today during independent drafting, four minutes each (three in 40/35-minute periods); one conference per learner across 8 to 10.

goal: Complete a coherent draft and plan revision after a private conference.
note: Read student drafts beside the model. Reach 650 to 1,000 words, connected sequence and reflective ending. Collect one conference record per student across drafting days 8 to 10; reuse it on day 14, never repeat the conference for assessment. Thirty learners: ten four-minute private conferences on each of days 8/9/10 during independent drafting, 40 teacher minutes per day, one record each; pairs draft independently while waiting. In 40/35-minute periods use ten three-minute conferences per day, 30 teacher minutes; prepared student revision notes carry the same evidence.

goal: Rewrite with a new approach and explain what the change gives the reader.
note: Reread Twain or Addams as structural model. W.5: student revision plan, changed opening/order, comparison of versions. Weekly analytic paragraph and sentence work are the revision explanation. No forced sharing of personal material. Conference rota: ten of 30 learners today during independent drafting, four minutes each (three in 40/35-minute periods); one conference per learner across 8 to 10.

goal: Publish a narrative and update it after feedback in a school device session.
note: Read narrative and peer feedback. W.6: each learner produces, publishes and updates using school tools, teacher posting, no student account; record actions once for day 14. Paper binder completes writing, but technology part stays unfinished until demonstrated. Edit all L.1/2 parts. Week 3, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: reflect / reflection / reflective (Latin flect/flex; re-; -ion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Read a new literary and memoir pair independently and write a source-based interpretation.
note: End part 1: unseen high-band poem/story and memoir on experience, to choose. Comprehension in both genres; paragraph applies an appropriate literary reading expectation and nonfiction expectation, W.9a/b. Word-log extract shows accurate use and independent gathering; reuse routine samples for long/short time frames and varied tasks/audiences. No routine scaffolds; access supports recorded separately.

goal: Write a compact reflective narrative from a new situation and defend usage choices.
note: End part 2: cold nonpersonal situation. A 300 to 450 word real/imagined narrative shows every W.3a to e part, including technique, significance, sequence, tone/outcome, detail and reflective closure. Edit and reference note cover grammar, changing/contested usage, capitalization, punctuation, hyphenation and spelling. Long process piece is separate.

goal: Lead a seminar and submit the process narrative with its revision and publishing record.
note: End part 3: student-led seminar on Twain/Addams/Frost, every SL.1a to d demand, including preparation, civil decisions, own goal/deadline/roles, probing/all positions, synthesis/contradictions/further research. Reuse days 8 to 10 one-on-one record. Narrative, revision plan and changed version show W.4/5; reuse day 11 digital publication/update record for W.6. Routine portfolio shows varied tasks/audiences and long/short writing. For 30 students, six simultaneous groups of five, teacher rotates as lead judge and checks the single observation record. Narrative/portfolio submission reuses prepared products; it is not another live performance.

goal: Use end evidence to repair a weak passage or extend an interpretation.
note: Read assessment and matching Twain/Addams/Frost passages. One response allocation for all end parts: targeted reading, narrative or usage groups; extension compares defensible Frost readings. Confirm independent long-book plan.

goal: Open Hamlet with a disputed report and distinguish textual uncertainty from missing background.
note: Read Hamlet 1.1 to 1.2 (g12-u2-01). Hook then retrieve e11-evidence-uncertain/e11-lit-themes. Retrieve e11-lit-word-tone, e11-word-strategies, e11-syntax-effect and e11-argument in short warm-ups across days 16 to 19. Content note: murder, grief, suicide and treatment of women; school support contacts, no disclosure or self-harm advocacy.

goal: Trace competing accounts of the Ghost and begin interacting themes.
note: Read Hamlet 1.3 to 1.5. Choose two themes without a tracker. Weekly paragraph distinguishes explicit detail, inference and unresolved matter. Full-play home reading in 20 to 30 minute portions; in-school reading alternative.

goal: Read inverted syntax for sense and verify a word whose older meaning changes a line.
note: Reread Hamlet 1.2/1.5 with Onions and Schmidt reference entries (g12-u2-03). Teach L.4a to d: context, word-change patterns, references for pronunciation/meaning/part of speech/etymology/usage, verification. L.3a: unpack/recombine syntax, consult an anchor reference and explain effect. Fold practice into 17/19 if needed. Week 4, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: reflect / reflection / reflective (Latin flect/flex; re-; -ion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Distinguish performance, inference and certainty among Hamlet observers.
note: Read Hamlet 2.1 to 2.2. Teach W.1a/b: significant precise literary claim, ordered argument map, fair/thorough counterclaim with strengths/limitations for audience knowledge, concerns, values and biases; relevant sufficient evidence across scenes.

goal: Discuss whether acting a part gives anyone reliable knowledge.
note: Reread Hamlet 2.2. Partner exchange and teacher-led seminar; two themes traced through interacting details with an objective summary distinct from interpretation.

goal: Explain how a soliloquy uses multiple meanings, figurative language and syntax.
note: Read Hamlet 3.1 with references. Literal/older meaning before connotation, tone, puns and fresh/beautiful language. Practise all L.4 strategies and L.3a. Suicide content note and support contacts; no advocacy for/against self-harm or imitation in a character voice.

goal: Test the play within the play as evidence and write a qualified interpretation.
note: Read Hamlet 3.2. Weekly paragraph weighs two strong readings and remaining uncertainty; sentence routine varies emphasis without changing evidence.

goal: Read the closet scene through discussion of language, action and gender.
note: Read Hamlet 3.3 to 3.4. Teacher-led discussion, the third SL.1 setting beside conferences/groups. Content note: murder, coercion, grief and treatment of Gertrude; no violent reenactment. Week 5, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: discern / discernment / discernible (Latin cern/cret; dis-; -ment/-ible); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Compare a silent film, audio and a live staging against the script.
note: Read Hamlet 3.4 beside corresponding Curio Class original silent-film segment, public-domain full-cast audio and brief live staging of nonviolent lines. Judge cuts/additions/emphasis/meaning against script evidence. Printed scene descriptions and teacher reading form the access path. Before the first version comparison, retrieve e11-lit-interpretations for two minutes with a supplied familiar script and contrasting interpretation; describe a difference, then evaluate its reading of the source.

goal: Refine a judgment about which performance choices the script supports.
note: Reread Hamlet 3.4 and its three versions. Brief replay, revised comparison chart, then a paragraph revised for one syntax effect with reference. Practice folds into 24/26 if needed; no assessed evidence removed.

goal: Track how political action complicates private revenge.
note: Read Hamlet 4.1 to 4.4; student-chosen theme interactions across the play. Content note: murder and its consequences.

goal: Read Ophelia scenes and disputed reports for what remains unknown.
note: Read Hamlet 4.5 to 4.7, including Ophelia songs within the whole play. Grief, death and suicide content note; no added graphic detail or personal disclosure. Weekly paragraph distinguishes report from certainty.

goal: Explain how the graveyard scene brings two themes together.
note: Read Hamlet 5.1. Objective summary separate from interpretation; trace theme development and interaction across the whole play. Death/burial content note. Week 6, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: discern / discernment / discernible (Latin cern/cret; dis-; -ment/-ible); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Complete the tragedy and lead a seminar on knowledge, choice and consequence.
note: Read Hamlet 5.2, completing the whole play. Student-led seminar sets goal/deadline/roles, synthesizes opposed readings and names needed research. Deaths/grief note, no violent reenactment.

goal: Read criticism as nonfiction and find the uncertainty it leaves open.
note: Read Coleridge Lecture on Hamlet excerpt (g12-u2-02) beside cited scenes. Distinguish explicit claims, inference and unresolved matter in nonfiction; assess the critic claim and its limits for a literary audience.

goal: Retrieve an American dramatist comparison beside Shakespeare interpretations.
note: Read supplied Trifles scene and two supplied versions beside Hamlet. Retrieve e11-lit-interpretations, last used grade 11; all materials supplied. Evaluate each version against source. Content note: abusive marriage and killing, no diagnosis or reenactment.

goal: Read a model argument and plan a significant claim with a fair counterclaim.
note: Read Curio Class model literary argument, to write, beside Hamlet/Coleridge. W.1a/b: argument map orders claims/counterclaims/reasons/evidence; weekly paragraph becomes opening rationale. Conference rota: ten of 30 learners today during drafting, four minutes each (three in 40/35-minute periods); record once across 32 to 34.

goal: Draft a literary argument that develops both sides for its intended reader.
note: Read model and drafts. Write toward 1,500 words; W.1b/c: develop claims/counterclaims fairly and thoroughly, strengths/limitations and audience biases, then link sections with varied transitions/syntax. Week 7, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: discern / discernment / discernible (Latin cern/cret; dis-; -ment/-ible); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. Conference rota: ten of 30 learners today during drafting, four minutes each (three in 40/35-minute periods); record once across 32 to 34. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Revise cohesion, literary style and a supported conclusion after feedback.
note: Read drafts against play/model. Teach W.1c/d/e and L.3a: varied cohesion, formal objective disciplinary style, supported conclusion; revise a paragraph for effect with a reference. One teacher conference per learner across 32 to 34 during drafting, reused on 37. Student revision plan. For 30 learners, days 32/33/34 each hold ten four-minute conferences during drafting; one record each, no extra assessment conference. In 40/35-minute periods use ten three-minute conferences per day, 30 teacher minutes; prepared student revision notes carry the same evidence.

goal: Interpret a new Shakespeare scene and critical passage without a supplied question.
note: End part 1: cold high-band soliloquy from a second Shakespeare play with sufficient scene context with enough surrounding text for two interacting themes, objective summary, explicit/inferred meaning and student-found uncertainty; cold nonfiction criticism for RI evidence/uncertainty. Annotated commentary includes figurative/connotative meanings, tone, multiple meanings and fresh/beautiful language. Texts to choose.

goal: Judge new interpretations and show how language strategies change a reading.
note: End part 2: unseen scene/script plus three short interpretations, each evaluated against source; day 31 Trifles product supplies American-dramatist evidence. Log covers all L.4a to d parts, including reference information and word changes. Syntax task unpacks a complex line and revises a paragraph for effect with reference. L.4b record includes discern/discernment/discernible: explain changed part of speech/meaning and use one form correctly in a new sentence; choose other strategies flexibly for unfamiliar words.

goal: Submit the complete literary argument with a reasoned conclusion.
note: End part 3: 1,500 word Hamlet argument product covers all W.1a to e, including significance, logical order, fair/thorough opposing claims, strengths/limitations, audience, cohesion, formal literary norms and supported close. Revision trail retained; reuse the one teacher-conference record from 32 to 34.

goal: Repair a weak inference, theme account or argument using end evidence.
note: Read assessment texts and student argument. One response allocation for the three end parts; targeted groups and extension on competing interpretation. This 23-day unit needs no mid-unit assessment. Week 8, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: discern / discernment / discernible (Latin cern/cret; dis-; -ment/-ible); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Open a sustained satire by separating persona from the view its details expose.
note: Read Swift A Modest Proposal (g12-u3-01), first half. Hook then retrieve e11-lit-irony, e11-lit-structure and e11-figurative-nuance; retrieve Hamlet ending from unit 2. Context is 1720s Irish poverty/hunger/colonial exploitation, not the later 1840s Great Famine. Content note: eating children is the persona proposal condemning cruelty, never a student imitation task.

goal: Prove the satirist real view from understatement and sustained persona.
note: Finish A Modest Proposal; reread turns/understatement. Teach L.5a, figures and role, including Hamlet paradox/hyperbole comparison. No satire about a real group suffering. Practice folds into 39/41 without cutting the complete text.

goal: Write a one-sitting analysis of how the Swift persona gives itself away.
note: Reread Swift. Short teacher-led seminar before essay. L.5b: compare near-synonyms for nuance in context. Taught writing, not an end assessment; no repeated cold comparative essay immediately before check 1.

goal: Explain how Austen narrator judgment depends on irony and near-synonyms.
note: Read Pride and Prejudice chapters 1 to 3 (g12-u3-02), home reading or in-school equivalent. L.5a/b: figures/role and contextual near-synonym nuance; prudent/sensible/amiable used only where selected passages support them. Independent readers may continue the whole novel. Pride and Prejudice chapters 1 to 3 now function as a literary anchor: return to narrator irony in 46/47 and the end script, rather than an optional book preview alone.

goal: Read a comedy opening for the class rules its wit tests.
note: Read Earnest act 1 (g12-u3-03), whole. Epigram/hyperbole/paradox in context and their comic role; class/marriage assumptions read in their time. Week 9, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: exclude / exclusion / exclusive (Latin claud/clus; ex-; -sion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Trace how comic complications depend on stated and intended meanings.
note: Read Earnest act 2, whole. Weekly paragraph on structural complication, whole meaning and aesthetic impact; sentence routine compares anchor/student syntax.

goal: Complete the comedy and explain what its resolution asks the audience to accept.
note: Read Earnest act 3, completing the whole play. Trace found-handbag ending through earlier details and its whole-structure/meaning/aesthetic effects.

goal: Compare tragic and comic endings and test a novel beginning and ending.
note: Reread Hamlet/Earnest endings and supplied Gatsby opening/closing pages, revisited in unit 4. The frame requires this preview; no Wolfsheim passage assigned early. Analyze beginning/ending choices, whole structure, meaning and aesthetic impact, not just plot differences. The weekly one-sitting analytic paragraph is the structural comparison, not an added assignment.

goal: Lead a seminar on how comedy and satire expose money and marriage rules.
note: Read Swift/Austen/Earnest passages. Student-led seminar sets goals/deadlines/roles, tests stated/meant and names unresolved research. Practice, no second scored discussion collection.

goal: Annotate a director commentary on an unfamiliar comic scene and endings.
note: End part 1: unfamiliar comic scene with alternative endings, plus the satirical passage used across days 48/49. One annotated director script distinguishes stated/meant, explains beginning/ending choices and their whole-structure, meaning and aesthetic effects, and explains contextual paradox/hyperbole roles and near-synonym nuance. Oral collection begins: four groups of up to four, five minutes per group, one minute per learner plus transitions. Hear 15 learners once today, the other 15 on 49; no repeat oral or separate second full written product. Teacher keeps one record per learner. In 50/40/35 minutes reserve 20 for groups, 5 for preparation and 25/15/10 for script work; waiting groups write.

goal: Explain how figures and near-synonyms alter an unfamiliar satirical passage.
note: End part 2: finish the same unfamiliar satirical/director script from 48; contextual figures and their role, near-synonym nuance and stated/meant, every L.5a/b part. Hear the remaining 15 learners once in four groups of up to four, five minutes per group with one-minute turns and transitions. Reuse day 48 records for learners already heard. In 50/40/35 minutes reserve 20 for groups, 10/5/5 for preparation and 20/15/10 for script completion. Each learner gives one oral explanation across the two-day window, never two.

goal: Revise a weak stated-versus-meant reading or structural explanation.
note: Read end texts/commentaries. One response allocation for both parts; extension tests a less obvious irony. Next unit retrieves grade 11 rows, no readiness check needed. Week 10, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: exclude / exclusion / exclusive (Latin claud/clus; ex-; -sion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Read a cold literary passage and essay on questions opened in units 1 and 2.
note: Check 1 part 1, week 11: unseen literary passage and literary nonfiction about experience/knowing/action, units 1/2 content. Integrated responses cite strong/thorough explicit and inferred evidence and find uncertainty in each genre; trace two literary themes, development/interaction and objective summary; explain contextual figurative/connotative meanings, a consequential multiple meaning and fresh/engaging/beautiful expression, and effects on meaning/tone. Select passages supporting every demand. Read both independently at high band, no routine supports; access supports separate. Reuse days 48/49 RL.5/RL.6 records without rescoring; these codes are absent from this new sample. New matrix form, no director-script or oral repeat.

goal: Write one literary argument using both cold literary and informational texts.
note: Check 1 part 2, week 11: first one-sitting two-text essay on day 51 pair, all W.1a to e and W.9a/b. Brief edit/reference note covers grammar, convention/change/contested choice, capitalization/punctuation/hyphenation/spelling. Teacher keeps time, no displayed timer. Reuse any prior conference record, no new one-to-one collection.

goal: Reteach the two weakest check demands and extend independent interpretations.
note: Read check 1 texts/evidence. One respond day; branch by two weakest demands, others test a defensible alternative. No repeated conference or preceding end-window product.

goal: Open Gatsby by questioning what its narrator chooses to reveal.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 1 (g12-u4-01). Hook then retrieve e11-lit-author-choices/e11-lit-american-periods. History unit 2 days 13 to 25 is earlier. If later/unpaired, 54/55 reserve two text-based context lessons on Great Migration, Prohibition and 1919 violence inside these days. Tom racist speech named as portrait of racism, never fact.

goal: Relate the valley of ashes to who pays for the dream.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 2 and Hughes I, Too (g12-u4-02), whole. Supplied Whitman excerpt retrieves grade 11. Conditional history bridge day 2, no added day. Content note: class, racism, coercion and violence toward Myrtle. I, Too opens the three-poem Harlem Renaissance anchor cluster; return to it beside McKay/Cullen on 64/66/68. Week 11, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: exclude / exclusion / exclusive (Latin claud/clus; ex-; -sion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Trace how delaying Gatsby introduction shapes reader judgment.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 3 and reread introductions in 1/2. Chapters 4/9 not assigned before day 57, keeping Wolfsheim after history Holocaust unit ends 56. Practice rereading folds into 55/57; whole chapter remains read.

goal: Separate narrator stereotyping from evidence in a character portrayal.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 4, first assigned now after 56. Antisemitic Meyer Wolfsheim portrayal named as stereotype in narration; align wording with history. Period slurs omitted with marks/editor notes and every omission disclosed; no silent rewriting or slurs spoken.

goal: Trace how a reunion changes the relation of past and present.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 5. Support beside original text. Begin staged home reading of long chapter 7 across the next nights, 20 to 30 minutes per school night; in-school equivalent supplied.

goal: Set modernist uncertainty beside a withheld personal history.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 6 and Eliot Prufrock (g12-u4-05), whole, with prior home read/in-school equivalent. Reread selected poem lines; weekly paragraph compares concealment/alienation and word choice. Gatsby lower measure but high qualitative demand. Prufrock now functions as a literary anchor; reread it with the novel on 61/66/68 to test withholding and self-presentation.

goal: Discuss how the confrontation depends on setting and sequence.
note: Finish Gatsby chapter 7. Teacher-led seminar tests competing narrator judgments. Content note: Myrtle violent death, coercion/racist speech, no reenactment or personal disclosure. Week 12, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: exclude / exclusion / exclusive (Latin claud/clus; ex-; -sion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Revise an account of how setting and character introductions work together.
note: Reread Gatsby chapter 7 and earlier settings. Fitzgerald cumulative sentence as reference; revise a paragraph for effect, L.3a. Practice folds into 60/62, no whole text or assessed work cut. Reread Prufrock beside the novel as well as the Fitzgerald syntax model.

goal: Explain the effect of telling a life history late in the novel.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 8. Trace reordered action and sympathy. Deaths/grief/violence content note, no graphic elaboration.

goal: Complete the novel and reconsider its beginning and ending as a whole.
note: Read Gatsby chapter 9, completing the whole novel. Revisit pages from unit 3. Antisemitic Wolfsheim portrayal/violent deaths named; content note matches 57, slur omissions marked.

goal: Read Harlem Renaissance voices in their historical and literary settings.
note: Read McKay If We Must Die, Cullen Yet Do I Marvel, and Toomer Cane excerpt (g12-u4-03/04/06). Poems whole; Toomer selection is November Cotton Flower in full, no other Cane section. Give 1919 racial-violence context before McKay, no extra violent imagery; paragraph compares answers to the dream. Hughes/McKay/Cullen form one three-poem literary anchor, counted once. Cane selection is the complete short section November Cotton Flower, not Karintha; reread its compressed social setting beside the three poems.

goal: Choose a period pair after reading a wider range of perspectives.
note: Read chosen option: Sugimoto A Daughter of the Samurai America chapters; Mena The Gold Vanity Set whole; Mourning Dove Cogewea chapter 1 (g12-u4-07 to 09). All options supplied/introduced, chosen text read in class or preceding home block. Name Japanese American/Mexican American/Native contexts without generalizing a people; contemporary Native nation context, disclosed slur omissions. Week 13, three-minute word-family slot inside existing vocabulary time: exclude / exclusion / exclusive (Latin claud/clus; ex-; -sion/-ive); compare meanings/parts of speech, use a changed form in a text-based sentence and verify with context/reference. Retrieve previously introduced families, no reteach week; use taught texts, never the cold assessment passage. In the same existing word block, retrieve grade 11 word-change forms from the supplied verified log for two minutes; use the coordinated grade 11 family list only when its day records confirm teaching. Five minutes total, no extra block.

goal: Lead a seminar comparing two chosen early twentieth-century texts on one theme.
note: Read student-selected pair from Gatsby/poems/Cane/choice set; Prufrock and the Hughes/McKay/Cullen cluster are returned-to anchors, with evidence in the comparison. Student-led seminar, goals/deadline/roles, evidence from both, further research need; no assigned pair.

goal: Place a twentieth-century work beside earlier American literature.
note: Read supplied brief Franklin/Wheatley excerpts for eighteenth century and Emerson/Douglass for nineteenth, beside selected twentieth-century work. Retrieve e11-lit-american-periods, last used grade 11. Explain period contexts and compare shared theme; no earlier copies assumed.

goal: Compare a chosen period pair and situate it across the American literature span.
note: End part 1: one-sitting comparison of student-chosen same-period pair plus concise eighteenth-/nineteenth-/twentieth-century account using day 67 sources. Period knowledge and similar-theme comparison demonstrated; cold transfer follows 69.
